title: A. Paññāvaddho: Meditation objects, or kammatthana, complement moral virtue by acting as solid posts to ground the mind in the present moment. Just as a…
content:
Meditation Objects (Kammatthana) as Essential Mental Anchors

Meditation objects, or kammatthana, complement moral virtue by acting as solid posts to ground the mind in the present moment. Just as a farmer knows that leaving livestock unconfined inevitably leads to destruction of crops and injury to the animals themselves, we must understand that a mind without the restraining influence of a meditation object will invariably create suffering for itself and others. This wandering tendency of the mind persists regardless of one's station in life. Whether you're young and vigorous or advanced in years, wealthy or struggling to make ends meet, highly educated or without formal schooling, living with physical limitations or blessed with robust health—if you lack the right meditation object, your mind remains relatively undeveloped. This condition isn't about intelligence or worldly accomplishments; it's about the fundamental inability to guide the mind toward calm and concentration. Despite whatever external success they might achieve, such people end their lives spiritually impoverished, having never experienced genuine mental well-being.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "I was talking with someone about time: past, future and present. He made the comment that the present is going past very quickly.…
content:
The Unchanging Present

"I was talking with someone about time: past, future and present. He made the comment that the present is going past very quickly. I thought to myself: It isn’t. The present doesn’t change. There's no change in the present. The present is just the present, and that’s all. The present moment is a personal thing inside oneself. The change is taking place externally. The change takes place in events and external things that arise and die away – but those things are more or less an illusion. The present doesn’t change. Everything round about is changing, but the present is a matter of the citta and that one doesn’t change."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "In order to learn how to think, behave and speak properly, we must train ourselves. We train ourselves to have a sharp mind,…
content:
The Threefold Training: Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā

"In order to learn how to think, behave and speak properly, we must train ourselves. We train ourselves to have a sharp mind, to understand the reasons for the things that happen in our lives, and thus to get to know ourselves properly. By getting to know ourselves, we get to know other people. By getting to know other people we learn how to behave rightly towards them—all because we know how to behave rightly within ourselves. The means to achieve this is the method that was taught by the Buddha, which is comprised of sīla or morality, samādhi or training of the mind, and paññā or wisdom. If we learn how to practice those three effectively, we can overcome the mental defilements, the kilesas, that cause the discontent we experience. As we overcome the kilesas, the discontent and suffering will lessen and eventually die away. This goal can be achieved. Many have done it already. Countless people have trained in sīla, samādhi and paññā and achieved very good results, experiencing high degrees of contentment and happiness. So the way to happiness is the way of sīla, samādhi and paññā."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "This renunciation is not simply a dreary denial of life's pleasures; it is the skillful use of our wisdom to recognize what really…
content:
Renunciation as the Discovery of Enduring Happiness

"This renunciation is not simply a dreary denial of life's pleasures; it is the skillful use of our wisdom to recognize what really brings happiness into our lives. When we see clearly how following the dictates of craving leads only to more and more desires, and realize that all we cling to is inherently unstable, we will be increasingly inclined to let go of those desires. When we truly understand the unreliability of worldly pleasures, we naturally turn toward what is reliable: the peace of a mind freed from wanting. This is not a teaching of despair but rather one of hope, for in releasing our grip on what cannot last, we open ourselves to a happiness that will endure. The practice of renunciation requires patient effort. Old mental habits do not disappear overnight, but through persistent contemplation of these truths, combined with practical steps to simplify our lives, we gradually experience the relief that comes with wanting less."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Avijja operates at a deeper level: it's our fundamental misunderstanding of reality, which prevents us from seeing things as they truly are, particularly…
content:
Distinguishing Root Ignorance from Proximate Craving

"Avijja operates at a deeper level: it's our fundamental misunderstanding of reality, which prevents us from seeing things as they truly are, particularly our ignorance concerning the true nature of impermanence, of not-self, and of the nature of suffering itself. This foundational ignorance conditions all subsequent mental formations, including the workings of tanha. The Buddha was primarily concerned with providing a practical path to liberation. By focusing on tanha in the Second Noble Truth, he identified something directly observable and workable. We can witness the effects of ceaseless craving in real time and begin examining them. The Third and Fourth Noble Truths then outline the final destination and the path to reach that goal. They reveal to us that suffering can end through the cessation of craving and show us how to achieve this objective."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "At a young age, we learned things from parents, from schoolmates, from school teachers—probably more from classmates than from teachers—and so on. We…
content:
The Influence of Early Childhood Education on Worldview

"At a young age, we learned things from parents, from schoolmates, from school teachers—probably more from classmates than from teachers—and so on. We learned our view of the world from the people around us. At that age, we were not in a position to judge the situation or to think “this is right” or “this is wrong”. We just accepted what we were told. We accepted everything from the normal worldly perspective. Naturally, parents teach their children the best they can. If they are good parents, they teach properly and in a good manner. They teach what they themselves learned from their mentors. But a lot of the knowledge that has been handed down is just views and supposition. There isn’t much proven truth in it. Not to blame the parents, but from the standpoint of Dhamma, it’s not the correct way to look at things. This misunderstanding occurs because people are convinced that the external world is what really matters. They believe that it’s very important to follow the mundane ways of the world. This happens because the defilements are strong, causing people to have more faith in the ways of the world than they do in the ways of Dhamma. As children, we begin to adopt this worldly outlook, which then forms the background of our thoughts and perceptions."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Meditation practise is like this too. We have to put our mind onto a particular object and keep it on that. At first…
content:
Cultivating Interest and Strength through Samādhi

"Meditation practise is like this too. We have to put our mind onto a particular object and keep it on that. At first the mind does not want to do it and it jumps about. Then after a time, as we put more effort into it and it becomes more habitual, the practise becomes a little more interesting, until we reach a point where we look forward to doing the meditation practise. At this stage a sense of happiness and contentment will arise in connection with our practice. This is the way of what we call “samādhi”, the meditation practice which makes the mind strong. The reason we develop samādhi is that when the mind is strong then we can develop wisdom."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: If a person decides to kill, he has malicious intention in his heart. When a person buys a piece of meat in the…
content:
Intention and Buying Meat

If a person decides to kill, he has malicious intention in his heart. When a person buys a piece of meat in the market, the attitude in his heart is entirely different; there is no intention to kill anything. For a bhikkhu, it’s an offense to eat meat only if we know, think, or suspect it was killed specifically for us. Westerners often make meat-eating a big issue because they look externally instead of looking inward at volition and heart. They don't consider the fundamental difference between killing and eating. The whole teaching of the Buddha points us to look inside and see what’s right for the heart.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The symbols we accumulate to structure the world around us are bound up with the faculty of memory. Memory is a database of…
content:
Memory as a Database for Pattern Recognition

The symbols we accumulate to structure the world around us are bound up with the faculty of memory. Memory is a database of all our previous experiences that runs like a continuous thread through the pattern of our mental activity. The data from memory comes in through the five senses; it’s the senses that tell us what to remember. An enormous amount of our thinking is based on memory. When we see or hear something, we identify it by comparing it to remembered impressions. Our present experience may be associated with external sensations, but those sensations have to be identified and interpreted in the light of past sensations. Once we recognize a particular sensation, we think about it, which again relies on the faculty of memory. For that reason, memory is an essential part of all of our perceptions. We can observe how some symbols in our minds tend to fade over time. They may be little used or outdated. But as soon as they start to disappear, up comes our self-identity, saying: I mustn’t let that one go. So we begin to think about it, in the process strengthening and reestablishing it in the mind. We refresh our memories by thinking.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The self is a reference point, and that reference point is created by the kilesas. Actually, we talk about self in terms of…
content:
Multiple Selves and the Senses

"The self is a reference point, and that reference point is created by the kilesas. Actually, we talk about self in terms of subject and object. When we sense things, there’s the one who senses and the thing that’s sensed. We see things: there’s the thing that’s seen and the one who sees it. We say, “I see that,” having assumed that there’s some self that sees it. “I hear it” or “I think it”—a self-perspective is always coming into our experience. But in each case, a different self arises. The self that relates to seeing is not the one that relates to hearing; the one that relates to the external senses is not the one that relates to thinking or to memory, et cetera. With each new mental state a different self arises, a different reference point. And every reference point is bound up with kilesas."
